robert-fortune.name: Robert Fortune
robert-fortune.summary: Scottish botanist and plant hunter (1812-1880) who introduced around 250 ornamental plants from China and elsewhere to Western gardens and helped develop India's tea industry.

darjeeling.name: Darjeeling
darjeeling.summary: A hill city in West Bengal, India, developed by the British as a summer retreat and later famous for tea plantations worked by labourers recruited from Nepal.

assam.name: Assam
assam.summary: A state in Northeast India along the Brahmaputra Valley, ruled by a succession of kingdoms including the Ahom kingdom from the 13th to early 19th century.

hotteok.name: Hotteok
hotteok.summary: A filled pancake popular as street food in South Korea, originating in Qing dynasty China and brought to Joseon Korea in the 19th century.

hakka-people.name: Hakka people
hakka-people.summary: A Han Chinese sub-ethnic group whose ancestral homes are spread across southern China's border regions, historically late arrivals from central China who settled remote, marginal lands.

meixian-meizhou.name: Meixian
meixian-meizhou.summary: A district of Meizhou Prefecture in Guangdong, China, an important Hakka settlement and ancestral home to many Hakka descendants worldwide.

second-opium-war.name: Second Opium War
second-opium-war.summary: A war from 1856 to 1860 in which Britain and France fought China's Qing dynasty over trade rights, ending in the forced legalization of the opium trade.

old-summer-palace.name: Old Summer Palace
old-summer-palace.summary: A complex of imperial palaces and gardens near Beijing, the main residence of Qing emperors from the 18th century until British and French troops destroyed it in 1860.

wu-changshuo.name: Wu Changshuo
wu-changshuo.summary: A Chinese calligrapher, painter and seal artist of the late Qing period, who lived from 1844 to 1927.

xiling-seal-engravers-society.name: Xiling Seal Engravers' Society
xiling-seal-engravers-society.summary: A Chinese arts organization in Hangzhou founded in 1904, one of the country's most important traditional stone seal-engraving associations.

haipai.name: Shanghai School (Haipai)
haipai.summary: An avant-garde 'East Meets West' cultural and artistic movement from Shanghai in the 20th and 21st centuries, blending Chinese and Western styles.

ren-bonian.name: Ren Bonian
ren-bonian.summary: A Chinese painter (1840–1896) who moved to Shanghai and became a leading member of the Shanghai School, noted for bold brushstrokes and ranked among the "Four Rens."

canton-porcelain.name: Canton porcelain
canton-porcelain.summary: A style of Chinese ceramic ware decorated in Guangzhou, made for export to Europe through what was, before 1842, the only legal port for Chinese trade with the West.

famille-rose.name: Famille rose
famille-rose.summary: A style of Chinese porcelain decoration dominated by pink overglaze enamel, introduced in the 18th century and reaching its finest quality during the Qianlong period.

james-bruce-8th-earl-of-elgin.name: Lord Elgin (8th Earl)
james-bruce-8th-earl-of-elgin.summary: A British colonial administrator and diplomat (1811-1863) who served as Viceroy of India and, during the Second Opium War, ordered the destruction of Beijing's Old Summer Palace in 1860.

eug-nie-de-montijo.name: Empress Eugénie
eug-nie-de-montijo.summary: Empress of the French from her 1853 marriage to Napoleon III until his overthrow in 1870, and briefly de facto head of state that same year; she later lived in exile in England.

palace-of-fontainebleau.name: Palace of Fontainebleau
palace-of-fontainebleau.summary: A large French royal château southeast of Paris used as a hunting lodge and residence by many French monarchs, later becoming a national museum.

guangxu-emperor.name: Guangxu Emperor
guangxu-emperor.summary: Tenth emperor of the Qing dynasty (1871-1908), whose 1898 reform program was crushed by Empress Dowager Cixi, after which he was held under house arrest until his death.

empress-dowager-cixi.name: Empress Dowager Cixi
empress-dowager-cixi.summary: Manchu noblewoman who controlled the Qing dynasty government as regent from 1861 until her death in 1908, suppressing reform efforts and placing the Guangxu Emperor under house arrest.

beiyang-fleet.name: Beiyang Fleet
beiyang-fleet.summary: A modernized Chinese navy of the late Qing dynasty, the largest fleet in Asia in the late 1880s, defeated in the 1894-95 First Sino-Japanese War.

summer-palace.name: Summer Palace
summer-palace.summary: An imperial garden complex in Beijing built for Empress Dowager Cixi, covering lakes, hills, palaces and thousands of historic buildings; named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.

boxer-rebellion.name: Boxer Rebellion
boxer-rebellion.summary: An anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising in North China (1899–1901) by the "Boxers," a martial-arts movement, ultimately defeated by an alliance of eight foreign powers.

eight-nation-alliance.name: Eight-Nation Alliance
eight-nation-alliance.summary: A coalition of eight nations whose troops invaded northern China in 1900 to relieve besieged foreign legations during the Boxer Rebellion, later occupying and looting Beijing.

qing-dynasty.name: Qing dynasty
qing-dynasty.summary: Manchu-led imperial dynasty of China from 1644 to 1912, the last imperial dynasty, which at its height controlled more territory than any other dynasty in Chinese history.

first-opium-war.name: First Opium War
first-opium-war.summary: War fought 1839–1842 between Britain and Qing China over the opium trade, ending in British victory, the Treaty of Nanking, and the cession of Hong Kong Island.

treaty-of-nanking.name: Treaty of Nanking
treaty-of-nanking.summary: 1842 peace treaty ending the First Opium War between Britain and Qing China; it ceded Hong Kong to Britain and opened five ports to trade.

century-of-humiliation.name: Century of humiliation
century-of-humiliation.summary: A Chinese historiographical concept for the period from the First Opium War (1839–1842) to the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, marked by foreign domination and territorial losses under the Qing dynasty.

edward-l-dreyer.name: Edward L. Dreyer
edward-l-dreyer.summary: American historian (1940–2007) known for his expertise on the history of China's Ming dynasty.

xinjiang.name: Xinjiang
xinjiang.summary: An autonomous region in northwestern China at the crossroads of Central and East Asia, historically called Chinese Turkestan, crossed by the Silk Road and home to Uyghurs and other ethnic groups.

sino-french-war.name: Sino-French War
sino-french-war.summary: An 1884–85 conflict between France and the Qing dynasty over influence in Vietnam, which ended with China ceding Vietnam as French protectorates.

treaty-of-tientsin.name: Treaty of Tientsin
treaty-of-tientsin.summary: Name for several 1858 treaties ending the first phase of the Second Opium War, opening more Chinese ports and effectively legalizing the opium trade.

convention-of-peking.name: Convention of Peking
convention-of-peking.summary: A set of three unequal 1860 treaties between Qing China and Britain, France and Russia that followed China's defeat in the Second Opium War.

bohai-sea.name: Gulf of Zhili
bohai-sea.summary: The 19th-century name for the Bohai Sea, a gulf on China's east coast near Beijing and the innermost extension of the Yellow Sea.

hanyang-arsenal.name: Hanyang Arsenal
hanyang-arsenal.summary: One of the largest and oldest modern weapons factories in Chinese history, located in Hanyang County.

battle-of-beicang.name: Battle of Beicang
battle-of-beicang.summary: A battle fought on 5 August 1900 during the Boxer Rebellion, in which the Eight Nation Alliance, led by Japanese forces, defeated the Qing dynasty army and forced it to retreat.

battle-of-yangcun.name: Battle of Yangcun
battle-of-yangcun.summary: A battle during the Eight-Nation Alliance's march from Tianjin to Beijing in the Boxer Rebellion, in which the Alliance defeated Qing forces and continued its advance.

gulab-singh.name: Gulab Singh
gulab-singh.summary: First maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir (1792–1857), originally a Sikh Empire commander who sided with the British and signed the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar establishing his state.

ladakh.name: Ladakh
ladakh.summary: A high-altitude region of the wider Kashmir area, now a union territory of India, historically important as a crossroads of trade routes.

imperial-examination.name: Imperial examination
imperial-examination.summary: Merit-based system for selecting Chinese state officials, formalized under the Tang and Song dynasties and lasting until its abolition in 1905.

herbert-giles.name: Herbert Giles
herbert-giles.summary: A British diplomat and sinologist who held the Chinese professorship at Cambridge for 35 years, devised the Wade–Giles romanization system, and translated Confucius and Lao Tzu, also publishing a Chinese–English dictionary in 1892; he lived 1845–1935.

a-history-of-chinese-literature.name: A History of Chinese Literature
a-history-of-chinese-literature.summary: An 1901 book by Herbert Giles, the first survey of Chinese literature to appear in English, containing extensive translations that let Chinese authors "speak for themselves."

new-culture-movement.name: New Culture Movement
new-culture-movement.summary: A Chinese sociopolitical movement of the 1910s-1920s that criticized traditional Confucian culture and promoted modern ideas, giving rise to the 1919 May Fourth Movement.

yan-fu.name: Yan Fu
yan-fu.summary: Chinese military officer, editor, and translator (1854–1921) best known for introducing Western ideas to China in the late 19th century.

lin-shu.name: Lin Shu
lin-shu.summary: Chinese writer (1852–1924) who introduced Western literature to Chinese readers, producing over 180 Classical Chinese translations despite knowing no foreign languages himself.

hu-shih.name: Hu Shih
hu-shih.summary: Chinese academic, writer, diplomat and politician (1891–1962) who championed written vernacular Chinese and Western-style democracy, later criticizing Mao Zedong and the Communist Party.

lu-xun.name: Lu Xun
lu-xun.summary: Chinese writer (1881–1936), pen name of Zhou Shuren, a leading figure of modern Chinese literature known for pioneering vernacular fiction and sharp, satirical essays.

liang-qichao.name: Liang Qichao
liang-qichao.summary: Chinese politician, journalist and intellectual (1873–1929) whose writings and reform movements strongly shaped political reform in modern China.

the-future-of-new-china.name: The Future of New China
the-future-of-new-china.summary: Unfinished 1902 novel by Liang Qichao imagining a utopian, wealthy, Confucian, constitutional-monarchy China in 1962 that had become a world power.

wu-jianren.name: Wu Jianren
wu-jianren.summary: Chinese writer (1866-1910) of the late Qing period known for novels such as The Sea of Regret, seen as a pioneer of modern Chinese fiction for his innovative narrators and centralized characters.

li-baojia.name: Li Baojia
li-baojia.summary: Qing-dynasty Chinese author (1867-1906), also known by his courtesy name Li Boyuan, who worked as a writer, essayist, calligrapher and periodical editor.

zeng-pu.name: Zeng Pu
zeng-pu.summary: Chinese novelist (1872–1935) and francophile of the late Qing era who studied French, worked in business and education, and later returned to writing.

zhongguo-wenxue-shi.name: Zhongguo Wenxue Shi
zhongguo-wenxue-shi.summary: A 1904 book by Lin Chuanjia, the first known published history of Chinese literature written in Chinese, focused mainly on classical prose.

lin-yutang.name: Lin Yutang
lin-yutang.summary: Chinese writer, linguist and inventor (1895–1976) known for bridging Chinese and Western culture, notably through My Country and My People, with six Nobel Literature nominations.

self-strengthening-movement.name: Self-Strengthening Movement
self-strengthening-movement.summary: A period of reform in China, about 1861 to 1895, under the late Qing dynasty following military defeats in the Opium Wars and Taiping Rebellion, aiming to modernize the military, economy and education.

h-c-zen.name: Ren Hongjun
h-c-zen.summary: Chinese politician, chemist and educator (1886–1961) who served as president of National Sichuan University and was a founding member and long-time president of the Science Society of China.

bing-zhi.name: Bing Zhi
bing-zhi.summary: A Chinese zoologist of Manchu ancestry (1886–1965) considered the founder of China's neontology and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

yuen-ren-chao.name: Zhao Yuanren
yuen-ren-chao.summary: A Chinese-American linguist, musician and polymath (1892–1982) who applied modern methods to Chinese phonology and helped create the Gwoyeu Romatzyh romanization system.

yang-xingfo.name: Yang Xingfo
yang-xingfo.summary: Chinese management scholar and activist (1893–1933) who co-founded the Science Society of China while studying at Cornell University.

taiping-rebellion.name: Taiping Rebellion
taiping-rebellion.summary: A 14-year civil war (1850–1864) between the Qing dynasty and the rebel Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, with death toll estimates ranging up to 100 million, making it one of history's deadliest civil wars.

kang-youwei.name: Kang Youwei
kang-youwei.summary: A Chinese political thinker and reformer (1858–1927) whose influence on the young Guangxu Emperor helped spark the failed Hundred Days' Reform of 1898.

hundred-days-reform.name: Hundred Days' Reform
hundred-days-reform.summary: A short-lived reform movement in China from June to September 1898, launched by the Guangxu Emperor with reformers Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao to modernize government, education and the military before conservatives ended it.

puyi.name: Puyi
puyi.summary: Last emperor of China, reigning as the Xuantong Emperor of the Qing dynasty (1908–1912, briefly restored in 1917), later installed as puppet ruler of Japanese-controlled Manchukuo and held as a war criminal after World War II.

1911-revolution.name: Xinhai Revolution
1911-revolution.summary: 1911 revolution that ended the Qing dynasty and over two millennia of Chinese imperial rule, leading to the founding of the Republic of China in 1912.

treaty-ports.name: Treaty ports
treaty-ports.summary: Sea ports in China, Japan and Korea opened to foreign trade in the 1800s, mainly through unequal treaties forced on those countries by Western powers.

hong-xiuquan.name: Hong Xiuquan
hong-xiuquan.summary: Chinese revolutionary and religious leader (1814 to 1864) who led the Taiping Rebellion against the Qing dynasty, declaring himself Heavenly King of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.

taiping-heavenly-kingdom.name: Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
taiping-heavenly-kingdom.summary: A theocratic monarchy (1851–1864) led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be Jesus Christ's younger brother, that sought to overthrow the Qing dynasty and ruled tens of millions of people in southern China.

chinese-empire-reform-association.name: Chinese Empire Reform Association
chinese-empire-reform-association.summary: A worldwide political group founded by reformer Kang Youwei in 1899 to unite overseas Chinese, restore the exiled Guangxu Emperor to power, and turn China into a constitutional monarchy.

celestial-empire.name: Celestial Empire
celestial-empire.summary: An archaic, literary name for China or the Chinese Empire, reflecting the emperor's status as the Son of Heaven, widely used in 19th-century English-language media.

zeng-guofan.name: Zeng Guofan
zeng-guofan.summary: Qing dynasty Chinese statesman and general (1811–1872) who raised the Xiang Army to help crush the Taiping Rebellion and restore the Qing Empire's stability.

chinese-empire.name: Chinese Empire
chinese-empire.summary: A Western term for the realm ruled by China's emperors, especially the Ming and Qing dynasties, spanning over two millennia of imperial rule beginning with unification under Qin in 221 BC.

nishi-amane.name: Nishi Amane
nishi-amane.summary: A Japanese philosopher (1829–1897) who studied law and economics in the Netherlands, advised Tokugawa Yoshinobu, served as a Meiji government bureaucrat, and co-founded the Meirokusha to introduce Western philosophy.

sexagenary-cycle.name: Sexagenary cycle
sexagenary-cycle.summary: A traditional Chinese 60-term cycle combining ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches, used since the Shang dynasty to record days and later years across East Asia.

plain-yellow-banner.name: Plain Yellow Banner
plain-yellow-banner.summary: One of the Eight Banners of Manchu military and society under the Qing dynasty, originally commanded personally by Nurhaci and later controlled directly by the emperor.

bordered-yellow-banner.name: Bordered Yellow Banner
bordered-yellow-banner.summary: One of the Eight Banners of Manchu military and society under the Later Jin and Qing dynasties, one of three Upper Banners under the emperor's direct command.

later-jin-1616-1636.name: Later Jin
later-jin-1616-1636.summary: A Jurchen-led dynasty established in Manchuria in 1616 by Nurhaci, renamed Great Qing in 1636 to begin the Qing dynasty.

robert-morrison-missionary.name: Robert Morrison
robert-morrison-missionary.summary: Robert Morrison: British Protestant missionary and pioneering sinologist who worked in Qing-era China, translated the whole Bible into Chinese over 25 years, and is called the 'Father of Anglo-Chinese Literature'.

thirteen-factories.name: Thirteen Factories
thirteen-factories.summary: A riverside neighborhood in Guangzhou, China, that from 1757 to 1842 was the sole legal site for most Western trade with China, repeatedly destroyed by fire during the Opium Wars.

thick-black-theory.name: Thick Black Theory
thick-black-theory.summary: A philosophical treatise written in 1911 by the disgruntled politician and scholar Li Zongwu, published the year the Qing dynasty was overthrown.

mary-porter-gamewell.name: Mary Porter Gamewell
mary-porter-gamewell.summary: American missionary, teacher, speaker and writer who founded a girls' school in Beijing in 1871, the first missionary sent to China by the Woman's Foreign Missionary Society; by the Boxer Rebellion it had 150 pupils.
